A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GeoDrag, with matching core methodology and experiments. The text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, allowing new material to be distinguished from relocated or duplicated content.

before.justification: v1 reports original DragBench evaluations, component and hyperparameter ablations, LoRA comparisons, runtime measurements, and a 60-participant user study.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds depth-robustness experiments, failure cases, runtime profiling, an optimized-variant comparison, and additional qualitative baseline comparisons.

M1.justification: Appendix L introduces an optimized variant that replaces dynamic BNNI updates with static four-neighbor interpolation and vectorizes latent relocation. The core geometry-aware field, spatial fusion, partitioning, and diffusion procedure remain unchanged.

E1.justification: DragBench and the point-based image-editing task are retained. Appendix J adds deliberately corrupted depth inputs as a distinct testing condition; the difficult-depth examples extend targeted scenario testing without establishing a new dataset or application domain.

E2.justification: SDEDrag and GoodDrag, previously cited but not evaluated as comparators, appear in the new qualitative comparison in Figure 20 and Appendix N. The quantitative comparator lineup in Table 1 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: New protocols include depth-range-scaled Gaussian perturbations, a displacement-scale sweep from 0.5 to 2.0, and stage-level timing and original-versus-optimized comparisons. Existing benchmark settings are retained. Profiling scope is inconsistent: Table 5 says full benchmark, while Appendix L specifies the Other Object subset.

E4.justification: Appendices J–M substantially expand diagnostic evaluation with noisy-depth robustness, difficult-depth cases, unseen-content failures, runtime bottleneck analysis, interpolation optimization, and displacement-scale sensitivity. The existing noise-injection ablation also gains a mountain example; its relocation and the moved component ablations are not new analyses.

E5.justification: The 60-participant user study and Figure 7 error bars are retained. The additions introduce no new seed counts, repeated-run reporting, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Gaussian depth perturbation defines a robustness experiment rather than an uncertainty estimator.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 and the user-study results are unchanged, but substantial robustness, timing, and qualitative findings are added. Table 4 reports an MD increase of 9.81 at the strongest depth noise. Table 6 reports original/optimized MD of 29.24/27.84, DAI1 of 0.128/0.133, and interpolation times of 0.2247/0.0014 seconds. These compare variants and conditions, not unchanged-setting version gains.

T1.justification: The projection derivation and core field equations are retained. v1 Appendix C.5's explicit definition relating DDIM noise scaling to the stochasticity parameter is omitted, while v2 Appendix J adds a mathematical specification of depth corruption. No new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same three central contributions: geometry-aware displacement, spatial plane modulation, and conflict-free partitioning. Claims concerning editing precision, structural consistency, efficiency, and multi-point control retain their scope.

C2.justification: Appendices J–M substantially extend interpretation beyond the earlier runtime-focused limitations paragraph. They explain compensation for unreliable depth, failures when interpolation must reconstruct unseen or overlapping content, possible error accumulation in dynamic interpolation, and distortion from excessive displacement scaling.

D1.justification: Appendix B's backbone, sampling settings, depth estimator, and hardware remain unchanged. v2 states that code is available rather than forthcoming and adds a project page. Appendices L–M document optimization details, stage timings, latent-coordinate rescaling, and a recommended scale of 1.2–1.3; they do not establish that the retained benchmark used a changed scale.

R1.justification: The bibliography and main related-work discussion are retained. Appendix N adds a specific comparative positioning against the already-cited SDEDrag and GoodDrag, particularly the efficiency contrast with GoodDrag's LoRA fine-tuning and iterative optimization.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative remain intact. v2 updates affiliations and conference information, adds declarations and an appendix contents list, moves existing ablation discussion into the main text, and organizes the additional material into Appendices J–N.

P2.justification: v2 adopts the ICLR layout, changes table typography and figure placement, promotes existing ablation displays into the main text, and adds four new diagnostic/comparison figures and three tables. The noise-injection display gains another example. v1 Figure 17 is also duplicated as v2 Figures 21 and 22.

improvement.justification: The new depth-robustness tests and explicit unseen-content failures improve assessment of GeoDrag's reliability and applicability, while the implementation analysis and added comparators provide useful supporting evidence. The net gain is limited by the timing-scope contradiction between Table 5 and Appendix L, duplicated Figures 21–22, and garbled failure-case prose. Table 6 also shows mixed accuracy effects, requiring qualification of the claimed optimization benefit.
